summary: Jamaica is a Caribbean island nation that became independent from Britain in 1962. It is the birthplace of reggae music and the Rastafari movement, and is also known for its top sprinters.

ranking.name: Protestant Christianity
ranking.description: After British rule began in 1655 the Anglican Church became the state church. From the late 18th century Baptist, Methodist and other missionaries reached deep into slave communities, combining preaching with the struggle for abolition, and Christianity thus spread among Black Jamaicans. In the 20th century, Pentecostal, Church of God and Seventh-day Adventist churches introduced from the United States grew rapidly, and today these churches have more members than the Anglican Church.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The share of non-religious people in Jamaica has risen in recent years, partly because of urbanization, young people's exposure to the internet and Western culture, and doubts about church authority. However, many who call themselves non-religious still believe in God or take part in folk beliefs, so it is not entirely the same as European-style secularization.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: During Spanish rule from 1494 to 1655 Catholicism was the official religion, but after the British took over, Catholicism was suppressed. In the late 19th century orders such as the Jesuits returned, exerting influence mainly in education; the followers include some Lebanese, Chinese and Indian-descended communities, but overall they are only a minority.

ranking.name: Rastafari
ranking.description: Rastafari arose in Jamaica in the 1930s, influenced by Marcus Garvey's "Back to Africa" ideas, and its followers regard Haile Selassie I, the Ethiopian emperor crowned in 1930, as the messiah. It resists colonial and racial oppression and became world-famous through the reggae singer Bob Marley in the 1970s, but true adherents are only a minority of the population, and in the early years they were suppressed by the government.

religion.background: The indigenous Taíno religion disappeared with the extinction of the population after Columbus's arrival in 1494 and Spanish colonization, and Spain brought Catholicism. In 1655 Britain seized Jamaica and the Anglican Church became the official church, but it mainly served white plantation owners. In the 18th–19th centuries Moravian, Baptist and Methodist missionaries preached to enslaved Africans, and the 1831 uprising led by the Black Baptist pastor Sam Sharpe accelerated abolition in 1834. African traditional beliefs fused with Christianity to produce religions such as Revival, and in the 1930s Rastafari arose. Today Jamaica is predominantly Protestant and is one of the countries with the highest density of churches per capita in the world.

ranking.name: Jamaican Creole (Patois)
ranking.description: The slaves transported from West Africa to Jamaica in the 17th–18th centuries came from different ethnic groups and could not understand each other's languages, so they could communicate only with the English vocabulary of the plantation owners, to which they added the sounds and vocabulary of African languages such as Akan, forming Patois. It is the mother tongue of the vast majority of Jamaicans at home and in daily life, and has spread around the world through reggae and dancehall music.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English has been Jamaica's official language since British rule began in 1655, and standard English is used in government, courts, schools and newspapers. Most Jamaicans occupy a continuous spectrum between Patois and English and switch according to the occasion, so those who speak English alone as their main language are actually a minority.

language.history: After Britain seized Jamaica in 1655, plantation owners imported large numbers of slaves from West Africa (mainly Akan, Igbo, Yoruba and other peoples), who on the plantations developed Jamaican Creole (Patois), built on English vocabulary and blending West African grammar and pronunciation. English was the language of the colonial government, schools and churches, and Patois was long regarded as "broken English" and discriminated against. After independence in 1962 English remained the sole official language, but reggae music, literature and broadcasting made Patois a symbol of Jamaican identity, and since the 2000s some groups have campaigned to make it an official language.

ranking.name: Ackee and saltfish
ranking.description: Ackee fruit flesh and salted cod soaked to remove the salt are sauteed together with onion, tomato and Scotch bonnet pepper, looking like scrambled eggs.
ranking.history: Ackee is native to West Africa and is generally thought to have reached Jamaica around 1778 on slave ships; salted cod was cheap protein imported from Newfoundland, Canada to feed slaves, while Jamaican rum and sugar were exported in the opposite direction. The pairing is thus a product of the Atlantic triangular trade and slavery. Unripe ackee is poisonous and can be eaten only after the fruit has opened naturally. It is regarded as Jamaica's national dish and is often a Sunday breakfast.

ranking.name: Jerk
ranking.description: Chicken or pork is marinated with allspice (Jamaica pepper), Scotch bonnet pepper, thyme and scallions, then slow-grilled over pimento wood, giving a spicy, smoky flavor.
ranking.history: The jerk technique derives from the indigenous Taíno method of smoking meat on wooden frames. In the 17th century the Maroons, who escaped the plantations and hid in the mountains, used this method to cook wild boar, marinating it with spices for preservation. The Maroons fought the British colonizers for a long time and in 1739 forced Britain to sign a treaty recognizing their autonomy, so jerk also symbolizes resistance. Today roadside oil-drum grills (jerk pans) are seen everywhere, and Boston Bay on Jamaica's west coast is regarded as the birthplace.

ranking.name: Jamaican patty
ranking.description: A half-moon pastry made of golden crust colored with curry powder or turmeric, filled with spicy ground beef, chicken or vegetables and baked. The crust is flaky and the filling spicy, and it is often tucked into coco bread for lunch.
ranking.history: The Jamaican patty blends the English Cornish pasty, the curry and spices brought by Indian indentured laborers, and the chili peppers loved by Africans. After slavery was fully abolished in 1838, Britain recruited indentured laborers from India to Jamaica from 1845, and curry powder thus entered the local diet. Today it is Jamaica's most common inexpensive lunch, and it also became popular in Britain and Toronto, Canada with immigration after the 1960s.
ranking.imageCredit: ritcharnd moskow from Toshi Station, USA・CC BY-SA 2.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Rice and peas
ranking.description: White rice and red kidney beans (called "peas" by Jamaicans) are cooked in coconut milk, with thyme, scallions and a whole chili pepper added for aroma.
ranking.history: Cooking rice and beans together comes from West Africa; slaves brought this way of eating to the Caribbean and replaced African ingredients with local beans and coconut. Although called "peas", it is mostly made with red kidney beans or pigeon peas. It is an essential side dish of the traditional Jamaican Sunday lunch, often served with roast chicken or curry goat.

ranking.name: Curry goat
ranking.description: Goat meat is marinated with curry powder, allspice and chili pepper and slow-stewed on the bone until tender, and served with white rice or rice and peas. The meat is soft and tender with a rich, spicy curry flavor, and it is a big-pot dish at parties.
ranking.history: From 1845 the British colonial government recruited tens of thousands of indentured laborers from India to Jamaica to fill the labor gap on plantations after abolition, and they brought curry cooking. Jamaicans replaced lamb with goat, which is easy to raise, and added local chili peppers and allspice, developing a distinctive curry goat. It is an indispensable main dish at weddings, birthday parties and "nine night" wake gatherings.
